# Interpreting Machine Learning models with the Responsible AI Dashboard

Lauri Lehman

13.12.2023

[Blog](https://zure.com/blog/tag/blog) [Data&AI](https://zure.com/blog/tag/dataai)

 ![](https://zure.com/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported_Blog_Media/Screenshot-from-2023-11-21-14-24-39-1024x290.png?width=1037&name=Screenshot-from-2023-11-21-14-24-39-1024x290.png)

Machine Learning (ML) models are often criticised for being hard to interpret. Many ML models are called "black-box" models, because there is no clear relationship between a model input ("feature") and the model output (prediction, score, etc.). From a technical viewpoint, this obscurity arises from the complexity and non-linearity of the model. This is particularly true for neural network models that may consist of billions of parameters, LLM models such as GPT-4 being the best examples.

Interpretation of complex ML models is not impossible, however! Techniques have already been developed to understand the behaviour of ML models and model interpretability is being actively researched in academia. In this post, I introduce some tools and techniques for model interpretation which are provided by the [Azure ML Responsible AI (RAI) Dashboard](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/machine-learning/concept-responsible-ai-dashboard).

The RAI Dashboard is a feature of the [Azure Machine Learning Service](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/machine-learning/) that assists Data Scientists and ML Engineers in understanding the model bias, interpreting the results given by the model (both globally and locally) and diagnosing the model errors. The features in the RAI Dashboard are designed for reducing the model bias based on people's personal traits, but it is also useful for understanding the model behaviour more generally and improving the overall accuracy of the model.

In this blog I will introduce the RAI Dashboard and show you how to get started with it. I also highlight some of the features in RAI Dashboard, such as error analysis and feature importance. You will also learn about cohort analysis and how it helps to understand and mitigate bias in ML models.

## Responsible AI Dashboard

Microsoft [released the RAI Dashboard back in December 2021](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/ai-machine-learning-blog/responsible-ai-dashboard-a-one-stop-shop-for-operationalizing/ba-p/3030944) and has since added multiple features to it, including [debugging of image recognition models](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/ai-machine-learning-blog/debug-object-detection-models-with-the-responsible-ai-dashboard/ba-p/3825658). The RAI Dashboard UI is part of Azure ML Studio, the graphical user interface to the Azure ML Service.

To start using the RAI Dashboard, you must first train a machine learning model and publish it to the Azure ML Service as a registered model. There are some additional requirements that the model has to satisfy so that a RAI Dashboard can be created for the model. The most important requirements are:

* The model is trained in Python using the [MLflow framework](https://mlflow.org/)
* The model is a regression or classification model from the [Scikit-learn library](https://scikit-learn.org)
* The input data used in analysis must be a Pandas DataFrame saved in Parquet format or a registered Dataset in Azure ML Service of type *MLTable*

Note that these requirements might change as the Azure ML Service evolves. See the official documentation for the [full list of current requirements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/machine-learning/concept-responsible-ai-dashboard#supported-scenarios-and-limitations).

## Creating a Responsible AI Dashboard

The RAI Dashboard can be created using the [Azure ML Studio UI](https://ml.azure.com), the Azure CLI command-line tool or the Azure ML Python SDK (v2). To create an RAI Dashboard, you must first train a machine learning model using the MLflow framework and the sklearn Python package and register the model in the Azure ML Service. If you don't have an ML model in this format, [see this Azure ML tutorial](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/machine-learning/how-to-train-scikit-learn) to train a model for testing purposes.

The RAI Dashboard is created by an Azure ML Pipeline Job that runs on an Azure ML Compute Cluster. Before creating an RAI Dashboard, you must therefore create a Compute Cluster to run jobs on. Follow [the instructions in Azure ML documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/machine-learning/how-to-create-attach-compute-cluster?view=azureml-api-2&tabs=azure-studio) to create a Compute Cluster, if you don't have one yet. I recommend to choose at least *STANDARD\_DS3\_V2* size for the Cluster, otherwise you might experience timeouts in Pipeline Job runs. Also make sure that the minimum number of nodes is set to 0 so that the compute capacity is scaled down after the Pipeline Job has finished.

Once the above requirements are met, the Dashboard can be created in Azure ML Studio UI by opening the previously registered ML model from the *Models* tab on the left. Then click on the *Responsible AI* tab in the model view and press the **Create Responsible AI Insights** button to start the Dashboard creation wizard.

 ![Responsible AI: How to create RAI Dashboard from Azure ML Studio UI](https://zure.com/hubfs/Imported_Blog_Media/Screenshot-from-2023-11-21-14-24-39-1024x290.png)   
 

Creating a Responsible AI Dashboard from the Azure ML Studio UI.

 

Follow the steps in the wizard to create the RAI Dashboard. You can use the same training and testing datasets that were used for training the model (given that they are in a format suitable for RAI Dashboard). You must also choose the model type that determines which components are available for the Dashboard. The following model types are supported at the time of writing:

* Regression
* Binary classification
* Multiclass classification

The content of the RAI Dashboard can be customized by changing the settings in the Dashboard creation wizard. Don't worry if you don't recognize all the concepts mentioned in the wizard, just add them using the default settings provided by the wizard. You can familiarize yourself with the new concepts by experimenting with different components after the Dashboard has been created.

The RAI Dashboard is always connected to a specific model registered in Azure ML Service. The data used in the analysis must also be defined at the creation time of the Dashboard. If you wish to analyse the model with a different dataset or analyse a new version of the model, a new version of the Dashboard must be created.

## Responsible AI Dashboard Components

 ![rai blog 2 2](https://zure.com/hubfs/Imported_Blog_Media/rai-blog-2-2.png) 

The RAI Dashboard consists of various components, such as:

* Error analysis
* Feature importance (global & local explanations)
* Counterfactuals
* Causal analysis

If the Dashboard is created from the Azure ML Studio UI, these components are included under the broader modules like *Model debugging* or *Real-life interventions*. If more granular control of the components is required, use the CLI or Python method to create the Dashboard and add the components one by one.

Note that using the RAI Dashboard for analysis requires an Azure ML Compute Instance, a managed virtual machine hosted in the Azure ML Service. [Follow these instructions to create your personal Compute Instance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/machine-learning/how-to-create-compute-instance) and start using the RAI Dashboard. If you want to be cost efficient, the size *STANDARD\_DS1\_V2* might be sufficient to run the analyses, but I recommend at least *STANDARD\_DS2\_V2* for a smooth experience.

## Error Analysis Component and Choosing a Cohort

In the following, I will use a case example from [Ruth Yakubu's RAI Dashboard sample repository](https://github.com/ruyakubu/RAI-Diabetes-Hospital-Readmission-classification) that uses the [UCI's Diabetes 130-US hospitals for years 1999–2008 dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Diabetes+130-US+hospitals+for+years+1999-2008) as source data. The ML model is trained to predict whether a diabetic patient will be readmitted back in a hospital in less than 30 days after being discharged. This is a binary classification model that uses all the available features in the dataset for training. [See this 3-part blog series from Ruth](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/ai-machine-learning-blog/how-to-create-a-responsible-ai-dashboard-to-debug-ai-models-part/ba-p/3766710) for a complete walkthrough of training the model and creating the RAI Dashboard.

The **Error analysis** component detects subsets of data points that have a particularly high error rate (see the screenshot below). In this example, the error rate for data points with *prior\_inpatient > 0* is 74/278 (26.62%) while the error rate for *prior\_inpatient = 0* is only 94/716 (13.13%), implying a 2-fold difference in error rate between two subsets of data. Furthermore, if we look at a subset with additional constraints: *11.50 < num\_medications <= 21.50*, the error rate increases up to 49/143 (34.27%). Thus, the Error analysis component of the RAI Dashboard helps to identify problems in the predictions of the model and concentrating on these issues might help to improve the model further.

 ![Screenshot from 2023 11 22 10 23 43](https://zure.com/hubfs/Imported_Blog_Media/Screenshot-from-2023-11-22-10-23-43-1024x488.png)   
 

Error analysis component in the Responsible AI Dashboard.

 

A subset of data that is defined by some constraint on the features of the dataset is called a *[cohort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohort_analysis)*. Cohorts are usually employed in statistical analysis to track certain user groups or target groups to understand their behaviour. Tracking the subgroups might reveal patterns that would otherwise be hidden under the behaviour of the general populus. The Error analysis component helps to identify cohorts that have a particularly high error rate. The error analysis component does not include time tracking of different cohorts, but you could always create your own analysis solution to track these cohorts, once they have been identified using the Error analysis component.

## Mitigating ML Model Bias

Generally, the difference in error rates is not necessarily caused by a bad model or bad data. In some cases, they might arise from the actual nature of the problem. Owing to the complexity of the illness, predicting the readmission status of patients might be genuinely more difficult if the patient has been hospitalised earlier and they have a certain number of medications prescribed. In any case, the most straightforward way of increasing model accuracy is usually adding more samples with similar values as those in the highest error cohort. Once a solid dataset has been gathered, it is also recommended to experiment with more complex models that might be able to better capture the details of the problem at hand.

The features that were discussed above are more related to the illness than the individual. If these features described personal traits of an individual, such as age or gender, and the error analysis shows that the model makes worse predictions for certain groups of individuals, it means that the model is biased towards this group and treats people unequally. This *accuracy bias* might be an artefact of the model or a consequence of a real-world phenomenon, such as unequal pay between genders or discrimination of elderly job applicants. It is the job of a data scientist to determine if the model can be improved to treat all people as equally as possible. Now, should the source data be manipulated so that the model gives the most equal outcome, in contrast to using real-world data with all its inherent biases? This is a hotly debated issue in the ethics of AI and I will withdraw from writing an opinion piece here!

The Error analysis component is just the starting point for analysing problems in the model. The RAI Dashboard contains many additional components and some of them are highlighted below, but a comprehensive review of all the features in the RAI Dashboard is outside the scope of this article.

## Understanding Bias with Cohort Analysis

 ![rai blog 3](https://zure.com/hubfs/Imported_Blog_Media/rai-blog-3-1024x1024.png) 

By exploring the components in the RAI Dashboard, we can dive deeper into the aspects of the ML model and discover possible sources of error. If we wish to understand better why the model performs poorly for a certain cohort, the cohort can be chosen as the "Global cohort" so that the analysis components use only data from this cohort for visualisations. The easiest way to create a cohort is to click on a node in the Error analysis component and click the *Save as a new cohort* button. The filters are set automatically to the values corresponding to the node. You can also create a cohort with arbitrary filters by pressing the *New cohort* button and defining the constraints manually.

You can create multiple cohorts and switch the active Global cohort to see different visualisations on the Dashboard. Some visualisations can also compare different cohorts, such as the Feature importances component shown below.

 ![Screenshot from 2023 11 23 15 20 42](https://zure.com/hubfs/Imported_Blog_Media/Screenshot-from-2023-11-23-15-20-42-1024x565.png)   
 

Feature importances for ML model.

 

Feature importance analysis tries to determine which features of the model are the most significant in predicting the outcome. A high feature importance value means that changing the feature value also changes the predicted value by a significant amount, or vice versa. Understanding which features are the most important for the model improves the interpretability of the model and advises which features we should concentrate on to improve the model. In the picture above, the *prior\_inpatient* feature is found to be the most significant feature in all cohorts. The second most significant feature, however, depends on the cohort.

Feature importance analysis can also identify features that are insignificant to the model. Whether these features should be included in the model, does not have a clear-cut answer and may depend on the case. In straightforward cases, adding more data for the model can increase the predictive power of the model. This might be the case if the features are independent and adding new features just gives more food for the model to consume, so to speak. Sometimes adding new features might complicate the model unnecessarily and actually decrease the quality of predictions. Again, the best advice is to experiment with different options to find the optimal solution.

## Additional features

Since the launch of the Responsible AI Dashboard, Microsoft has released some new features to the Dashboard. In addition to the standard regression and classification tasks, it is now also possible to analyse free text models with the [Responsible AI text dashboard](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/machine-learning/how-to-responsible-ai-text-dashboard) and image detection models with the [Responsible AI image dashboard](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/machine-learning/how-to-responsible-ai-image-dashboard). Such features usually require writing a custom solution. With the RAI Dashboard, these tasks can be performed without writing any code or with only a small coding effort, allowing data scientists to focus on their core tasks.

Another useful feature is the [Responsible AI Scorecard](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/machine-learning/concept-responsible-ai-scorecard). Data scientists often present their findings to team members or management using visualisations. Crafting these presentations can be a tedious and time-consuming task. The RAI Scorecard feature provides tools for creating a neat presentation based on similar components as in the RAI Dashboard. These insights can be exported to a PDF file to be shared with team members and stakeholders. This is another feature that takes data scientists time off from non-essential tasks and helps them to concentrate on core analysis. [See this blog post](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/ai-machine-learning-blog/responsible-ai-dashboard-and-scorecard-in-azure-machine-learning/ba-p/3391068) for comprehensive instructions how to create the RAI Scorecard.

Note that the features mentioned in this section are still in the preview stage when this article is written and are therefore not recommended for production use.

## Summary

In this article, I have highlighted some of the features and capabilities provided by the Responsible AI Dashboard. There are several advantages why it is worth spending some time learning to use the RAI Dashboard:

* Useful not only for reducing model bias, but also for debugging general errors and improving overall accuracy
* Very little coding (or none at all) is required to create the RAI Dashboard
* Fully customisable, choose only the components that are relevant for the use case
* Supports various use cases like classification, free text analysis and image detection
* Results can be shared easily in PDF format with the RAI Scorecard
* Spend more time doing the analysis instead of creating analysis scripts and making presentations

Lauri Lehman

args.summary:
This blog post by Lauri Lehman (published December 13, 2023) introduces the Azure ML Responsible AI (RAI) Dashboard, a tool for interpreting and debugging machine learning models, particularly "black-box" models like neural networks. The RAI Dashboard helps data scientists understand model bias, interpret results globally and locally, and diagnose errors.

**Key Requirements for Use:**
- Model must be trained in Python using MLflow framework
- Must be a regression or classification model from Scikit-learn
- Input data must be Pandas DataFrame in Parquet format or MLTable dataset in Azure ML

**Dashboard Components:**
- Error analysis (detects subsets with high error rates)
- Feature importance (global & local explanations)
- Counterfactuals
- Causal analysis

**Case Example:** Using UCI's Diabetes 130-US hospitals dataset, the error analysis component showed that patients with prior_inpatient > 0 had a 26.62% error rate vs. 13.13% for those with prior_inpatient = 0. Adding constraints (11.50 < num_medications <= 21.50) increased the error rate to 34.27%.

**Additional Features:**
- Responsible AI text dashboard for free text models
- Responsible AI image dashboard for image detection models
- Responsible AI Scorecard for exporting findings to PDF
- Cohort analysis for comparing subgroups

The dashboard can be created via Azure ML Studio UI, Azure CLI, or Azure ML Python SDK (v2). It requires a Compute Cluster (recommended STANDARD_DS3_V2) and a Compute Instance for analysis (recommended STANDARD_DS2_V2).

# What is Responsible AI?

**APPLIES TO:** ![](media/yes.png?view=azureml-api-2) [Azure CLI ml extension v2 (current)](how-to-configure-cli?view=azureml-api-2) ![](media/yes.png?view=azureml-api-2) [Python SDK azure-ai-ml v2 (current)](https://aka.ms/sdk-v2-install)

Responsible Artificial Intelligence (Responsible AI) is an approach to developing, assessing, and deploying AI systems safely, ethically, and with trust. AI systems result from many decisions made by their creators. Responsible AI helps guide these decisions—from defining system purpose to user interaction—toward more beneficial and equitable outcomes. It keeps people and their goals at the center of design and respects values like fairness, reliability, and transparency.

Microsoft created a [Responsible AI Standard](https://blogs.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/prod/sites/5/2022/06/Microsoft-Responsible-AI-Standard-v2-General-Requirements-3.pdf), a framework for building AI systems based on six principles: fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, and accountability. These principles are the foundation of a responsible and trustworthy approach to AI, especially as intelligent technology becomes more common in everyday products and services.

This article explains how Azure Machine Learning provides tools to help developers and data scientists implement and operationalize these six principles.

![ Diagram of the six principles of Microsoft Responsible AI, which encompass fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, and accountability.](media/concept-responsible-ai/concept-responsible-ml.png?view=azureml-api-2)

## Fairness and inclusiveness

AI systems should treat everyone fairly and avoid affecting similar groups differently. For example, when AI systems provide guidance on medical treatment, loan applications, or employment, they should make the same recommendations to people with similar symptoms, financial circumstances, or qualifications.

**Fairness and inclusiveness in Azure Machine Learning**: The [fairness assessment](concept-fairness-ml?view=azureml-api-2) component of the [Responsible AI dashboard](concept-responsible-ai-dashboard?view=azureml-api-2) helps assess model fairness across sensitive groups, such as gender, ethnicity, age, and other characteristics.

## Reliability and safety

To build trust, AI systems must operate reliably, safely, and consistently. They should function as designed, respond safely to unexpected conditions, and resist harmful manipulation. Their behavior and ability to handle different conditions reflect the range of situations developers anticipated during design and testing.

**Reliability and safety in Azure Machine Learning**: The [error analysis](concept-error-analysis?view=azureml-api-2) component of the [Responsible AI dashboard](concept-responsible-ai-dashboard?view=azureml-api-2) helps you:

* Get a deep understanding of how failure is distributed for a model.
* Identify cohorts (subsets) of data with a higher error rate than the overall benchmark.

These discrepancies can occur when the system or model underperforms for specific demographic groups or for rarely observed input conditions in the training data.

## Transparency

When AI systems inform decisions that impact people's lives, it's critical that people understand how those decisions are made. For example, a bank might use an AI system to decide if a person is creditworthy, or a company might use one to select job candidates.

A crucial part of transparency is *interpretability*: providing useful explanations of AI system behavior. Improving interpretability helps stakeholders understand how and why AI systems work, so they can identify performance issues, fairness concerns, exclusionary practices, or unintended outcomes.

**Transparency in Azure Machine Learning**: The [model interpretability](how-to-machine-learning-interpretability?view=azureml-api-2) and [counterfactual what-if](concept-counterfactual-analysis?view=azureml-api-2) components of the [Responsible AI dashboard](concept-responsible-ai-dashboard?view=azureml-api-2) help generate human-understandable descriptions of model predictions.

The model interpretability component provides several views into a model's behavior:

* *Global explanations*. For example, what features affect the overall behavior of a loan allocation model?
* *Local explanations*. For example, why was a customer's loan application approved or rejected?
* *Model explanations for a selected cohort of data points*. For example, what features affect the overall behavior of a loan allocation model for low-income applicants?

The counterfactual what-if component helps you understand and debug a machine learning model by showing how it reacts to feature changes and perturbations.

Azure Machine Learning also supports a [Responsible AI scorecard](how-to-responsible-ai-scorecard?view=azureml-api-2). The scorecard is a customizable PDF report that developers can configure, generate, download, and share with technical and non-technical stakeholders. It helps educate stakeholders about dataset and model health, achieve compliance, and build trust. The scorecard can also support audit reviews by revealing machine learning model characteristics.

## Privacy and security

As AI becomes more common, protecting privacy and securing personal and business information is more important and complex. Privacy and data security require close attention because AI systems need data to make accurate predictions and decisions. AI systems must comply with privacy laws that:

* Require transparency about the collection, use, and storage of data.
* Mandate that consumers have appropriate controls to choose how their data is used.

**Privacy and security in Azure Machine Learning**: Azure Machine Learning enables administrators and developers to [create secure configurations](concept-enterprise-security?view=azureml-api-2) that comply with company policies. With Azure Machine Learning and the Azure platform, you can:

* Restrict access to resources and operations by user account or group.
* Restrict incoming and outgoing network communications.
* Encrypt data in transit and at rest.
* Scan for vulnerabilities.
* Apply and audit configuration policies.

Microsoft also created two open-source packages to help implement privacy and security principles:

* [SmartNoise](https://github.com/opendifferentialprivacy/smartnoise-core): Differential privacy is a set of systems and practices that help keep the data of individuals safe and private. In machine learning solutions, differential privacy might be required for regulatory compliance. SmartNoise is an open-source project (co-developed by Microsoft) that contains components for building differentially private systems that are global.
* [Counterfit](https://github.com/Azure/counterfit/): Counterfit is an open-source project that comprises a command-line tool and generic automation layer to allow developers to simulate cyberattacks against AI systems. Anyone can download the tool and deploy it through Azure Cloud Shell to run in a browser, or deploy it locally in an Anaconda Python environment. It can assess AI models hosted in various cloud environments, on-premises, or in the edge. The tool is agnostic to AI models and supports various data types, including text, images, or generic input.

## Accountability

People who design and deploy AI systems must be accountable for how those systems operate. Organizations should use industry standards to develop accountability norms. These norms help ensure that AI systems are not the final authority on decisions that affect people's lives and that humans maintain meaningful control over highly autonomous systems.

**Accountability in Azure Machine Learning**: [Machine learning operations (MLOps)](concept-model-management-and-deployment?view=azureml-api-2) is based on DevOps principles and practices that improve AI workflow efficiency. Azure Machine Learning provides these MLOps capabilities for better accountability:

* Register, package, and deploy models from anywhere. You can also track the associated metadata that's required to use the model.
* Capture the governance data for the end-to-end machine learning lifecycle. The logged lineage information can include who is publishing models, why changes were made, and when models were deployed or used in production.
* Notify and alert on events in the machine learning lifecycle. Examples include experiment completion, model registration, model deployment, and data drift detection.
* Monitor applications for operational issues and issues related to machine learning. Compare model inputs between training and inference, explore model-specific metrics, and provide monitoring and alerts on your machine learning infrastructure.

In addition, the [Responsible AI scorecard](concept-responsible-ai-scorecard?view=azureml-api-2) in Azure Machine Learning creates accountability by enabling cross-stakeholder communication. The scorecard empowers developers to configure, download, and share model health insights with both technical and non-technical stakeholders. Sharing these insights helps build trust.

Azure Machine Learning also supports decision-making by informing business decisions through:

* Data-driven insights, which help stakeholders understand causal treatment effects on outcomes using historical data only. For example, "How would a medicine affect a patient's blood pressure?" These insights come from the [causal inference](concept-causal-inference?view=azureml-api-2) component of the [Responsible AI dashboard](concept-responsible-ai-dashboard?view=azureml-api-2).
* Model-driven insights, which answer user questions (such as "What can I do to get a different outcome from your AI next time?") so they can take action. These insights are provided through the [counterfactual what-if](concept-counterfactual-analysis?view=azureml-api-2) component of the [Responsible AI dashboard](concept-responsible-ai-dashboard?view=azureml-api-2).

## Next steps

* For more information on how to implement Responsible AI in Azure Machine Learning, see [Responsible AI dashboard](concept-responsible-ai-dashboard?view=azureml-api-2).
* Learn how to generate the Responsible AI dashboard via [CLI and SDK](how-to-responsible-ai-dashboard-sdk-cli?view=azureml-api-2) or [Azure Machine Learning studio UI](how-to-responsible-ai-dashboard-ui?view=azureml-api-2).
* Learn how to generate a [Responsible AI scorecard](concept-responsible-ai-scorecard?view=azureml-api-2) based on the insights observed in your Responsible AI dashboard.
* Learn about the [Responsible AI Standard](https://blogs.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/prod/sites/5/2022/06/Microsoft-Responsible-AI-Standard-v2-General-Requirements-3.pdf) for building AI systems according to six key principles.

# What is Responsible AI - Azure Machine Learning

[View original resource](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/machine-learning/concept-responsible-ai?view=azureml-api-2)

Microsoft's Responsible AI Standard isn't just another set of aspirational principles. It's a practical framework deeply integrated into Azure Machine Learning that helps organizations build AI systems with built-in safeguards. This resource stands out because it bridges the gap between high-level responsible AI concepts and hands-on implementation, offering concrete tools and workflows that developers and data scientists can use immediately within the Azure ecosystem.

## The Six Pillars in Action

Microsoft's framework is built on six core principles, but what makes this resource valuable is how it translates each principle into actionable practices:

* **Fairness** goes beyond bias detection to include fairness assessment tools, bias mitigation algorithms, and performance comparison across demographic groups. Azure ML provides built-in fairness metrics and visualization dashboards.
* **Reliability and Safety** encompasses robust testing frameworks, model validation pipelines, and continuous monitoring capabilities. The platform includes error analysis tools and model debugging features.
* **Privacy and Security** integrates differential privacy techniques, secure multi-party computation, and data encryption throughout the ML lifecycle, not just as an afterthought.
* **Inclusiveness** focuses on dataset representation analysis, inclusive design practices, and accessibility considerations in AI system outputs.
* **Transparency** provides model interpretability tools, automated documentation generation, and explainable AI features that work across different model types.
* **Accountability** establishes clear governance processes, audit trails, and responsibility matrices that track decision-making throughout model development and deployment.

## What Makes This Different from Other Frameworks

Unlike purely theoretical responsible AI frameworks, Microsoft's approach is tightly coupled with actual tooling. You're not just reading about responsible AI principles. You're getting access to:

* **Integrated toolsets** like Fairlearn for bias assessment and InterpretML for model explainability
* **Automated compliance checks** that run as part of your ML pipeline

# Cloud Pricing Comparison: AWS vs Azure vs GCP (2026 Technical Cost Modeling Guide)

This comprehensive guide from Usage.ai (updated June 12, 2026) provides a detailed technical cost comparison across AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform, covering compute, storage, Kubernetes, serverless, and commitment discount structures.

## Key Findings

**Compute Pricing (On-Demand):** For equivalent 4 vCPU/16 GB RAM Linux instances in US-East, on-demand pricing is nearly identical across all three providers at approximately $0.19/hr. GCP's e2-standard-4 is cheaper ($0.134/hr) but uses variable processor allocation and is not performance-equivalent for CPU-bound workloads.

**ARM Instances:** All three providers offer ARM-based instances at approximately 20% lower on-demand pricing than equivalent x86 instances (AWS Graviton2 at $0.154/hr, Azure D4ps v5 at ~$0.154/hr, GCP Tau T2A at ~$0.154/hr).

**Commitment Discounts:** 
- 1-year commitments: 30-40% off on-demand
- 3-year commitments: 50-65% savings
- AWS Savings Plans: up to 66% off (Compute), up to 72% (EC2 Instance)
- Azure Hybrid Benefit: up to 85% off for Windows workloads when combined with Reserved VMs
- GCP resource-based CUDs: up to 55% off for standard machine series on 3-year terms
- GCP Sustained Use Discounts: automatic, up to 30% off for N1 instances running full month

**Storage Pricing (Standard Hot Tier, US-East):**
- AWS S3 Standard: $0.023/GB/month
- Azure Blob Hot (LRS): $0.018/GB/month
- GCP Cloud Storage Standard: $0.020/GB/month

**Egress:** GCP charges 33% more than AWS and 38% more than Azure for internet egress ($0.12/GB vs $0.09/GB on AWS).

**Kubernetes Control Planes:** AKS is free; EKS and GKE Standard cost $73/month per cluster.

## Critical Insight: Coverage Ratio Matters More Than Discount Percentage

The guide emphasizes that commitment coverage ratio (the percentage of eligible workload usage protected by discounted commitments) is the largest cost lever. A 55% discount at 85% coverage produces ~47% overall savings, not 55%, because the uncovered 15% pays on-demand rates. The blended effective rate formula is: (Covered Usage × Discounted Rate + Uncovered Usage × On-Demand Rate) ÷ Total Usage.

## Decision Framework

- **Windows/Microsoft workloads:** Azure is cheapest due to Hybrid Benefit
- **Stable full-month workloads:** GCP's automatic SUDs give it an edge
- **AI/ML & analytics:** GCP (BigQuery/Vertex AI), Azure (OpenAI/GPT-4 integration), AWS (broadest GPU selection)
- **Containerized/Kubernetes:** AKS (free control plane), GKE Autopilot (per-pod pricing)
- **Multi-cloud:** No universally cheapest provider; commitment strategy and risk management matter more than provider choice

## Usage.ai Platform

Usage.ai offers commitment automation with products including Autopilot (autonomous commitment management), Insured Commitments (cashback/credits for underutilization), CoPilot (GCP/Azure coverage), and Flex Commitments (AWS-specific). The platform charges a percentage of realized savings only, with $0 fee if no savings achieved.

Cloud storage pricing involves five distinct cost dimensions: storage capacity, API operations, data retrieval, data transfer out (egress), and replication/cross-region transfer. Real-world spend can be 2-5x higher than raw storage rates.

Operations are categorized as Class A, Class B, Class C, Class D, or Free. Costs vary by storage class, location type, and namespace (flat vs. hierarchical). - **Metadata**: Object metadata is always accessible, even when the object is archived.

- **Minimum size**: No minimum object size requirement.

- **Durability/availability**: Matches the standard Object Storage tier.

# Amazon EBS Pricing Guide (2026)

## Core Pricing Concept
EBS charges for **provisioned** storage capacity, not actual data used. A 500 GB volume with 10 GB of data costs the same as one with 490 GB of data. Charges accrue from volume creation until deletion, regardless of whether the volume is attached to a running instance. EBS charges appear under "EC2-Other" in Cost Explorer, not as a separate line item.

## EBS Volume Types & Pricing (us-east-1, 2026)

| Type | Price/GB-month | Best For |
|------|---------------|----------|
| **gp3** | $0.08 | Most workloads (default) |
| **gp2** | $0.10 | Legacy - migrate to gp3 |
| **io2 Block Express** | $0.125 | Mission-critical databases |
| **io1** | $0.125 | Previous gen - io2 preferred |
| **st1** | $0.045 | Big data, ETL, log processing |
| **sc1** | $0.015 | Infrequent access, cold data |

**Key gp3 details:** Base price includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s throughput. Additional IOPS at $0.005/IOPS-month above 3,000; additional throughput at $0.06/MiB/s-month above 125 MiB/s.

## Snapshot Pricing
- **Standard tier:** $0.05/GB-month (incremental - only changed blocks billed)
- **Archive tier:** $0.0125/GB-month (75% cheaper, 90-day minimum retention, $0.03/GB retrieval fee)
- **Fast Snapshot Restore:** $0.75/DSU-hour (billed per minute with 1-hour minimum)
- Snapshots are **never automatically deleted** when you terminate an instance or volume

## Hidden Costs
1. **Stopped instances:** EBS volumes continue billing at full rate when EC2 is stopped
2. **Orphaned snapshots:** Accumulate indefinitely without lifecycle policies
3. **ASG scale-in orphans:** Non-root volumes left behind after Auto Scaling group terminates instances
4. **60-second minimum:** Volumes deleted within 60 seconds still billed for 60 seconds
5. **Forgotten FSR:** Fast Snapshot Restore charges continue until explicitly disabled

## gp2 → gp3 Migration Savings
- gp3 at 1 TB: $80/month vs gp2 at 1 TB: $100/month (20% savings)
- For workloads needing 6,000 IOPS: gp2 requires 2,000 GB ($200/month) vs gp3 with 1 TB + 6,000 IOPS ($95/month)
- Migration is zero-downtime via Elastic Volumes

## Cost Optimization Levers
1. Migrate gp2 to gp3 (highest ROI)
2. Archive/delete unused snapshots via AWS Data Lifecycle Manager (free)
3. Find and delete unattached volumes
4. Right-size io1/io2 IOPS provisioning

## Notable New Features (2025-2026)
- **Volume Clones (GA Oct 2025):** Instant point-in-time copies at $0.00080/GB of written blocks
- **io2 Block Express auto-upgrade:** All io2 volumes upgraded April 2025 with tiered IOPS pricing
- **Free Tier:** 30 GB storage, 2M I/Os, 1 GB snapshot storage (12 months); new accounts also get up to $200 in credits

- 50 GB gp3 boot + 500 GB gp3 data + 200 GB snapshots = **$54/month**

# The Complete Guide to Amazon EFS: Features, Pricing, and Use Cases

This guide (published April 3, 2025) provides a comprehensive overview of **Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)** — a fully managed, cloud-native file storage service from AWS. EFS offers simple, scalable, elastic file storage using the NFS protocol, designed for workloads that need to share data across multiple instances or containers simultaneously.

## Key Features
- **Elastic and Scalable:** Automatically expands/shrinks from gigabytes to petabytes without manual intervention
- **High Performance:** Two performance modes — General Purpose (low latency, default) and Max I/O (high throughput for parallel workloads)
- **Security:** Encryption at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS 1.2); IAM integration; VPC security groups; EFS Access Points for fine-grained permissions
- **Durability:** Regional (multi-AZ) with 11 nines durability; One Zone option for cost savings (~47% cheaper)
- **Lifecycle Management:** Automatic tiering between Standard, Infrequent Access (IA), and Archive storage classes
- **Fully Managed:** No provisioning or maintenance required

## File System Types
- **Regional (Recommended):** Data stored across multiple AZs for highest durability
- **One Zone:** Single AZ, cheaper but less durable; suitable for dev/test workloads

## Throughput Modes
- **Elastic Throughput (default):** Automatically scales based on demand, pay per GB read/written
- **Provisioned Throughput:** Fixed capacity purchased (~$6/1 MB/s per month in us-east-1)

## Pricing (US East N. Virginia)
- **Standard storage:** ~$0.30/GB-month
- **IA storage:** ~$0.016/GB-month (92% cheaper)
- **Archive storage:** ~$0.008/GB-month (97% cheaper)
- **Read operations:** ~$0.03/GB; **Write operations:** ~$0.06/GB
- **Lifecycle transitions:** ~$0.01-0.03/GB
- **Free Tier:** 5 GB Standard storage free for 12 months for new accounts

## Use Cases
- Web and content management (shared file stores across server fleets)
- Enterprise applications (ERP, home directories, NAS replacement)
- Database backups and disaster recovery
- Container storage (ECS, EKS, Fargate persistent volumes)
- Analytics and machine learning (shared datasets for training jobs)

## Comparison with Other AWS Storage Services
- **EFS vs EBS:** EFS is shared NAS across multiple instances; EBS is block storage attached to a single instance. EBS offers lower latency but no multi-instance sharing.
- **EFS vs S3:** EFS is a POSIX file system with file-level access; S3 is object storage via REST API. S3 is cheaper per GB ($0.023 vs $0.30) but lacks file system semantics.
- **EFS vs FSx:** FSx offers specialized file systems (Windows SMB, Lustre for HPC, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS) with advanced features; EFS is simpler, more general-purpose, and serverless.

# Understand Azure Files Billing

This Microsoft Learn article explains the billing models, cost factors, and total cost of ownership considerations for Azure Files. The content is structured around four key cost factors: billing model, media tier, redundancy option, and resource model.

## Billing Models

Azure Files supports three billing models:
1. **Provisioned v2 (recommended)**: Separately provision storage, IOPS, and throughput. Pay for what you provision regardless of actual usage. Recommended for all new deployments.
2. **Provisioned v1**: Provision storage; IOPS and throughput are computed from storage amount. Only available for SSD (premium) tier.
3. **Pay-as-you-go**: Usage-based billing for storage, transactions, and data transfers. Only available for HDD (standard) storage.

## Media Tiers & Redundancy

- **SSD (premium)**: High performance, low latency, single-digit millisecond latency.
- **HDD (standard)**: Cost-effective general-purpose storage.

Four redundancy options: LRS (local), ZRS (zone), GRS (geo, HDD only), GZRS (geo-zone, HDD only).

## Provisioned v2 Model Details

- Minimum provisioned storage: 32 GiB
- Maximum: 256 TiB (262,144 GiB)
- SSD min IOPS: 3,000; max: 102,400
- HDD min IOPS: 500; max: 50,000
- SSD min throughput: 100 MiB/sec; max: 10,340 MiB/sec
- HDD min throughput: 60 MiB/sec; max: 5,120 MiB/sec
- **Guardrails**: IOPS/throughput capped at 5x recommended values based on provisioned storage to prevent unnecessary costs.
- **Bursting**: Credit-based IOPS bursting allows temporary spikes above provisioned IOPS on a best-effort basis.
- Supports both classic file shares (Microsoft.Storage) and top-level file shares (Microsoft.FileShares) resource models.

## Provisioned v1 Model Details

- Only for SSD premium tier.
- Minimum: 100 GiB; Maximum: 100 TiB.
- IOPS formula: MIN(3000 + 1 × ProvisionedStorageGiB, 102400)
- Throughput formula: 100 + CEILING(0.04 × ProvisionedStorageGiB) + CEILING(0.06 × ProvisionedStorageGiB)
- Supports credit-based bursting (free) and paid bursting (optional, usage-based).
- Snapshots billed at reduced rate regardless of unused provisioned space.

## Pay-as-you-go Model Details

- Only HDD (standard) storage, classic file shares.
- Three access tiers: Transaction optimized, Hot, Cool.
- Tiers differ in storage price vs. transaction price ratios.
- Transactions categorized as: Write, List, Read, Other/Protocol, Delete.
- Switching tiers incurs transaction and data retrieval charges.
- Best practice: Start in transaction optimized during migration, then optimize access tier based on post-migration usage patterns.

## Key Considerations for Cost Planning

- Use base-2 units (KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB).
- Reservations offer up to 36% discount on storage.
- Azure Files is fully managed; value-added services (Azure Backup, Azure File Sync, Microsoft Defender for Storage) have additional costs.
- Soft delete and snapshots have specific billing implications under each model.
- Storage account limits (shared across shares) require careful capacity planning for 3-5 years.

# Cloud & AI Storage Pricing Comparison 2026: AWS, Azure, GCP, OCI

This article from Finout (published April 20, 2026) provides a comprehensive breakdown of cloud storage pricing across the four major providers — AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle OCI — with a focus on hidden costs beyond the headline per-GB rate.

## Why Storage Costs Are Hard to Predict
Cloud storage pricing involves five distinct cost dimensions: storage capacity, API operations, data retrieval, data transfer out (egress), and replication/cross-region transfer. Real-world spend can be 2-5x higher than raw storage rates.

## Pricing Summary (May 2026, US Regions, Single-Region Redundancy)

| Provider | Hot/Standard | Infrequent Access/Cool | Cold | Archive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AWS S3 | $0.023/GB (first 50 TB) | $0.0125/GB (S3 Standard-IA) | $0.004/GB (Glacier Instant) | $0.00099/GB (Deep Archive) |
| Azure Blob | $0.018/GB (Hot, LRS) | $0.010/GB (Cool) | $0.0045/GB (Cold) | $0.00099/GB (Archive) |
| Google Cloud | $0.020/GB (Standard) | $0.010/GB (Nearline) | $0.004/GB (Coldline) | $0.0012/GB (regional Archive) |
| Oracle OCI | $0.0255/GB (Standard) | $0.015/GB (Infrequent Access) | — | $0.0026/GB (Archive) |

## Key Provider Details

**AWS S3:** Multiple tiers with volume discounts. Hidden costs include request charges (PUT $0.005/1,000; GET $0.0004/1,000), egress ($0.09/GB first 10TB), and minimum storage durations (30-180 days). A 100TB S3 Standard workload goes from $2,304/month on paper to ~$3,200 with requests and egress.

**Azure Blob:** Four-tier model with Cold tier ($0.0045/GB) splitting the difference between IA and Glacier. Redundancy multiplies costs significantly — GRS is roughly 2x LRS. A 128 KiB minimum billable object size applies to Cool, Cold, and Archive tiers.

**Google Cloud:** Simplest structure of the big four. Notable 2026 changes: Nearline multi-region pricing increased (to $0.015/GB), Archive multi-region decreased (to $0.0024/GB in US/EU). Inter-region traffic within same multi-region is free for reads.

**Oracle OCI:** Most expensive hot tier ($0.0255/GB) but includes 10 TB/month free egress and charges only $0.0085/GB beyond that — roughly 10x cheaper than AWS egress. Best for egress-heavy workloads.

## New AI Storage Pricing (2026)

**AWS S3 Vectors:** Purpose-built for vector embeddings (RAG, semantic search). $0.06/GB/month storage, $0.20/GB uploads, plus query charges. AWS claims up to 90% cost reduction vs. traditional vector DBs.

**AWS S3 Tables (Apache Iceberg):** For analytical tabular data. $0.0265/GB/month (15% above S3 Standard), plus $0.05/GB processed for maintenance operations — teams have reported 20x bill increases from forgetting this.

**Training/Inference Data:** Best practice is lifecycle policies — Standard during active training, Intelligent-Tiering/Nearline for 90 days after, Glacier/Archive after that. A 500 TB training bucket can drop from $11,500/month to ~$2,800/month with proper tiering.

## Hidden Costs
1. Egress fees (often exceed storage charges)
2. Request charges (log-heavy buckets can spend 2x on requests vs. storage)
3. Retrieval fees ($0.02-$0.05/GB on archive tiers)
4. Minimum storage durations (30-180 days)
5. Minimum object size charges (Azure 128 KiB, GCP 128 KB)
6. Redundancy costs (GRS roughly doubles rates)
7. Cross-service integration tools that also cost money

## FinOps Best Practices
1. Allocate before optimizing (use Virtual Tags for cost ownership)
2. Automate lifecycle policies
3. Monitor access patterns, not just storage size
4. Model total cost (storage + requests + egress + retrieval)
5. Apply unit economics

Cloud storage pricing involves five distinct cost dimensions: storage capacity, API operations, data retrieval, data transfer out (egress), and replication/cross-region transfer. Real-world spend can be 2-5x higher than raw storage rates.

### Data Storage
Storage is charged per gibibyte-hour, prorated to the sub-second. Storage classes include Standard, Nearline, Coldline, Archive, and Rapid Cache/Rapid Storage, with varying costs depending on location type (Region, Dual-region, Multi-region, Zonal).

**Region pricing (per GiB/hour):**
- Standard: $0.000027397 (~$0.020/GB/month)

- Coldline: $0.000005479 (~$0.004/GB/month)
- Archive: $0.000001644 (~$0.0012/GB/month)
- Rapid Cache: $0.0001233

**Minimum storage durations:** Nearline (30 days), Coldline (90 days), Archive (365 days). Early deletion incurs charges as if stored for the minimum duration.

### Operation Charges
Operations are categorized as Class A, Class B, Class C, Class D, or Free. Costs vary by storage class, location type, and namespace (flat vs. hierarchical). For example, in a single region with Standard storage: Class A operations cost $0.005/1,000 operations (flat) or $0.0065 (hierarchical); Class B operations cost $0.0004/1,000 (flat) or $0.0005 (hierarchical).

### Retrieval Fees
Applied when reading data from Nearline ($0.01/GiB), Coldline ($0.02/GiB), or Archive ($0.05/GiB). No retrieval fees for Standard, Rapid, or Autoclass-enabled buckets.

- **Within Google Cloud:** Free within same location. Between regions, costs range from $0.02/GiB (within Northern America or Europe) to $0.14/GiB (to Latin America).
- **General (internet) usage:** Free inbound. Outbound to worldwide destinations: $0.12/GB (0-10 TiB), $0.11/GB (10-150 TiB), $0.08/GB (150+ TiB). Higher rates for China and Australia.

### Autoclass
Management fee of $0.0025 per 1,000 objects per 30 days. One-time enablement charge for reclassifying existing objects.

### Storage Intelligence
Standard tier: $2.5 per million objects per month. 30-day trial tier available. Early termination fee applies if removed within 30 days.

- **Inventory Reports:** $0.0025-$0.0028 per million objects
- **Rapid Cache:** Cache ingest ($0.0032/GiB), cache operations ($0.0002/1,000), cache data transfer out ($0.0006/GiB). Cache storage per Rapid Cache rates above.
- **Rapid Bucket (zonal):** Data transfer out ($0.0006/GiB), data transfer in ($0.0032/GiB). Storage per Rapid storage rates.
- **Object Contexts:** $3 per million objects per month
- **Bucket Relocation:** $0.04/GB for data moved, plus applicable charges per source/destination matrix.

- **Data retrieval**: To access archived data, you must restore it to Object Storage. Restored data is available for download for a default of 24 hours, customizable from 1 to 240 hours. After the window expires, data returns to its archived state. Restore operations cannot be done by object prefix.

- **Metadata**: Object metadata is always accessible, even when the object is archived.

- **Minimum size**: No minimum object size requirement.

- **Durability/availability**: Matches the standard Object Storage tier.

# Amazon EBS Pricing Guide (2026)

## Core Pricing Concept
EBS charges for **provisioned** storage capacity, not actual data used. A 500 GB volume with 10 GB of data costs the same as one with 490 GB of data. Charges accrue from volume creation until deletion, regardless of whether the volume is attached to a running instance. EBS charges appear under "EC2-Other" in Cost Explorer, not as a separate line item.

## EBS Volume Types & Pricing (us-east-1, 2026)

| Type | Price/GB-month | Best For |
|------|---------------|----------|
| **gp3** | $0.08 | Most workloads (default) |
| **gp2** | $0.10 | Legacy - migrate to gp3 |
| **io2 Block Express** | $0.125 | Mission-critical databases |
| **io1** | $0.125 | Previous gen - io2 preferred |
| **st1** | $0.045 | Big data, ETL, log processing |
| **sc1** | $0.015 | Infrequent access, cold data |

**Key gp3 details:** Base price includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s throughput. Additional IOPS at $0.005/IOPS-month above 3,000; additional throughput at $0.06/MiB/s-month above 125 MiB/s.

## Snapshot Pricing
- **Standard tier:** $0.05/GB-month (incremental - only changed blocks billed)
- **Archive tier:** $0.0125/GB-month (75% cheaper, 90-day minimum retention, $0.03/GB retrieval fee)
- **Fast Snapshot Restore:** $0.75/DSU-hour (billed per minute with 1-hour minimum)
- Snapshots are **never automatically deleted** when you terminate an instance or volume

## Hidden Costs
1. **Stopped instances:** EBS volumes continue billing at full rate when EC2 is stopped
2. **Orphaned snapshots:** Accumulate indefinitely without lifecycle policies
3. **ASG scale-in orphans:** Non-root volumes left behind after Auto Scaling group terminates instances
4. **60-second minimum:** Volumes deleted within 60 seconds still billed for 60 seconds
5. **Forgotten FSR:** Fast Snapshot Restore charges continue until explicitly disabled

## gp2 → gp3 Migration Savings
- gp3 at 1 TB: $80/month vs gp2 at 1 TB: $100/month (20% savings)
- For workloads needing 6,000 IOPS: gp2 requires 2,000 GB ($200/month) vs gp3 with 1 TB + 6,000 IOPS ($95/month)
- Migration is zero-downtime via Elastic Volumes

## Cost Optimization Levers
1. Migrate gp2 to gp3 (highest ROI)
2. Archive/delete unused snapshots via AWS Data Lifecycle Manager (free)
3. Find and delete unattached volumes
4. Right-size io1/io2 IOPS provisioning

## Notable New Features (2025-2026)
- **Volume Clones (GA Oct 2025):** Instant point-in-time copies at $0.00080/GB of written blocks
- **io2 Block Express auto-upgrade:** All io2 volumes upgraded April 2025 with tiered IOPS pricing
- **Free Tier:** 30 GB storage, 2M I/Os, 1 GB snapshot storage (12 months); new accounts also get up to $200 in credits

# AWS EFS Cost Guide 2026: Pricing & Optimization

## Overview
This guide (published May 29, 2026, by Benjamin Thomas) explains how AWS EFS pricing works, where costs silently inflate, and seven strategies engineering teams can use to reduce EFS spend without sacrificing performance.

## Key Pricing Structure (US East Regions)
- **EFS Standard (Regional)**: $0.30/GB-month
- **EFS One Zone Standard**: $0.16/GB-month
- **EFS Infrequent Access (IA)**: $0.016/GB-month
- **EFS One Zone IA**: $0.0133/GB-month
- **EFS Archive**: $0.008/GB-month
- **Provisioned Throughput**: ~$6/MB/s-month beyond baseline
- **Cross-AZ transfer**: ~$0.01/GB

## Billing Dimensions
EFS billing is multi-dimensional: storage (GB-month), throughput (Elastic or Provisioned), data access/tiering activity, and cross-AZ data transfer. Additional fees apply for IA/Archive reads/writes and tier transitions. Archive has a 90-day minimum storage duration. Small files in IA/Archive are metered with a minimum billing size of 128 KiB.

## Five Common Cost Pitfalls
1. **Unmonitored file systems** – unused systems quietly accrue charges
2. **Mis-tiering of data** – cold data kept in expensive Standard tier
3. **Throughput mismatch** – wrong mode for workload patterns
4. **Cross-AZ hidden transfer costs** – unnoticed data-path charges
5. **Lack of tagging/visibility** – no cost ownership or attribution

## Seven Optimization Strategies
1. **Choose the right storage class** – IA reduces storage cost ~94% vs Standard
2. **Implement lifecycle management** – auto-transition data after inactivity (14, 30, 60, 90 days)
3. **Monitor and rightsize** – delete unused files, compress large files
4. **Align throughput mode** – Elastic for variable, Provisioned only for sustained high throughput
5. **Optimize data transfer** – consolidate operations, use caching layers
6. **Automate FinOps governance** – cost alerts, tagging, idle environment shutdown
7. **Evaluate alternatives** – S3 for read-heavy analytics, EBS for low-latency block, FSx for Lustre for HPC

## Key Statistics
- ~$44.5 billion in enterprise cloud infrastructure waste projected for 2026 (~21% of spend)
- 71% of developers skip spot orchestration; 61% do not rightsize; 58% don't use reserved instances
- Enterprises take an average of 31 days to identify cloud waste; ~25 days to rightsize
- McKinsey observed 28% of cloud spend is wasted
- 62% of developers want more control over cloud costs but lack visibility
- Sedai claims up to 50% cloud cost savings, 75% performance gains, 6× productivity improvements
- Sedai has managed over 100,000 production operations without incident
- One security company (Palo Alto Networks) saved $3.5M using Sedai

## Tools for Monitoring
AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, AWS Pricing Calculator, CloudWatch, EFS Intelligent-Tiering, third-party FinOps platforms, and Sedai's autonomous optimization platform.

## Conclusion
Continuous, autonomous governance is the most sustainable way to control cloud costs at scale. Manual quarterly audits are insufficient; automated monitoring, simulation, and enforcement are needed to keep pace with cloud evolution.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: The Complete Guide to Amazon EFS: Features, Pricing, and Use Cases ---

<summary>
# The Complete Guide to Amazon EFS: Features, Pricing, and Use Cases

This guide (published April 3, 2025) provides a comprehensive overview of **Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)** — a fully managed, cloud-native file storage service from AWS. EFS offers simple, scalable, elastic file storage using the NFS protocol, designed for workloads that need to share data across multiple instances or containers simultaneously.

## Key Features
- **Elastic and Scalable:** Automatically expands/shrinks from gigabytes to petabytes without manual intervention
- **High Performance:** Two performance modes — General Purpose (low latency, default) and Max I/O (high throughput for parallel workloads)
- **Security:** Encryption at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS 1.2); IAM integration; VPC security groups; EFS Access Points for fine-grained permissions
- **Durability:** Regional (multi-AZ) with 11 nines durability; One Zone option for cost savings (~47% cheaper)
- **Lifecycle Management:** Automatic tiering between Standard, Infrequent Access (IA), and Archive storage classes
- **Fully Managed:** No provisioning or maintenance required

## File System Types
- **Regional (Recommended):** Data stored across multiple AZs for highest durability
- **One Zone:** Single AZ, cheaper but less durable; suitable for dev/test workloads

## Throughput Modes
- **Elastic Throughput (default):** Automatically scales based on demand, pay per GB read/written
- **Provisioned Throughput:** Fixed capacity purchased (~$6/1 MB/s per month in us-east-1)

## Pricing (US East N. Virginia)
- **Standard storage:** ~$0.30/GB-month
- **IA storage:** ~$0.016/GB-month (92% cheaper)
- **Archive storage:** ~$0.008/GB-month (97% cheaper)
- **Read operations:** ~$0.03/GB; **Write operations:** ~$0.06/GB
- **Lifecycle transitions:** ~$0.01-0.03/GB
- **Free Tier:** 5 GB Standard storage free for 12 months for new accounts

## Use Cases
- Web and content management (shared file stores across server fleets)
- Enterprise applications (ERP, home directories, NAS replacement)
- Database backups and disaster recovery
- Container storage (ECS, EKS, Fargate persistent volumes)
- Analytics and machine learning (shared datasets for training jobs)

## Comparison with Other AWS Storage Services
- **EFS vs EBS:** EFS is shared NAS across multiple instances; EBS is block storage attached to a single instance. EBS offers lower latency but no multi-instance sharing.
- **EFS vs S3:** EFS is a POSIX file system with file-level access; S3 is object storage via REST API. S3 is cheaper per GB ($0.023 vs $0.30) but lacks file system semantics.
- **EFS vs FSx:** FSx offers specialized file systems (Windows SMB, Lustre for HPC, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS) with advanced features; EFS is simpler, more general-purpose, and serverless.

The guide concludes with a section promoting Cloudchipr, a cloud cost optimization platform.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: AWS Backup Pricing ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/backup/pricing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an AWS documentation page detailing the pricing structure for AWS Backup, a service that allows users to centralize and automate backup management across AWS services. The page covers multiple pricing components:

**Backup Storage Pricing**: Pay only for backup storage used (per GB-month), with no minimum fees or setup charges. Storage tiers include warm and cold storage options, with cold storage currently supported for EBS, EFS, DynamoDB, Timestream, SAP HANA on EC2, and VMware Backup. Minimum retention periods apply (90 days for cold storage, 60 days for warm storage tier transitions).

**Restore Pricing**: Billed based on the amount of data restored per month (measured in GB). Different rates apply for standard and warm storage restores, vary by resource type (EBS, EFS, S3, DynamoDB, etc.), and cold storage restores incur additional charges.

**Restore Testing Pricing**: Charges based on the number of recovery points tested ($1.50 per recovery point) and the amount of storage restored. Restore testing storage charges mirror standard restore pricing.

**Cross-Region Data Transfer Pricing**: Billed when transferring data between AWS Regions, with rates varying by resource group (EFS, DynamoDB, Timestream, VMware = Group 1; S3, Aurora DSQL, EKS = Group 2; EBS, FSx, Storage Gateway, DocumentDB, Neptune, Aurora, RDS = Group 3).

**Backup Search Pricing**: Based on number of objects/files scanned, with charges for indexing, storage of indexes, and search operations.

**AWS Backup Audit Manager Pricing**: Based on backup evaluations and configuration items recorded by AWS Config.

**Malware Protection Pricing**: Provided by Amazon GuardDuty, priced per GB of data scanned per month.

**Access Point Pricing**: Charges for API requests (GET, HEAD, LIST) and data retrieval for S3 Access Points attached to backup recovery points.

The page includes five detailed pricing examples covering: (1) an all-in scenario with EFS backups, copies, restores, and evaluations; (2) AWS Backup for S3 with 500 TB data and GET/LIST/PUT API charges; (3) restore testing for EBS and EFS backups; (4) logically air-gapped vault copies between US East and EU West; and (5) backup search with EBS volumes.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Understand Azure Files Billing

This Microsoft Learn article explains the billing models, cost factors, and total cost of ownership considerations for Azure Files. The content is structured around four key cost factors: billing model, media tier, redundancy option, and resource model.

## Billing Models

Azure Files supports three billing models:
1. **Provisioned v2 (recommended)**: Separately provision storage, IOPS, and throughput. Pay for what you provision regardless of actual usage. Recommended for all new deployments.
2. **Provisioned v1**: Provision storage; IOPS and throughput are computed from storage amount. Only available for SSD (premium) tier.
3. **Pay-as-you-go**: Usage-based billing for storage, transactions, and data transfers. Only available for HDD (standard) storage.

## Media Tiers & Redundancy

- **SSD (premium)**: High performance, low latency, single-digit millisecond latency.
- **HDD (standard)**: Cost-effective general-purpose storage.

Four redundancy options: LRS (local), ZRS (zone), GRS (geo, HDD only), GZRS (geo-zone, HDD only).

## Provisioned v2 Model Details

- Minimum provisioned storage: 32 GiB
- Maximum: 256 TiB (262,144 GiB)
- SSD min IOPS: 3,000; max: 102,400
- HDD min IOPS: 500; max: 50,000
- SSD min throughput: 100 MiB/sec; max: 10,340 MiB/sec
- HDD min throughput: 60 MiB/sec; max: 5,120 MiB/sec
- **Guardrails**: IOPS/throughput capped at 5x recommended values based on provisioned storage to prevent unnecessary costs.
- **Bursting**: Credit-based IOPS bursting allows temporary spikes above provisioned IOPS on a best-effort basis.
- Supports both classic file shares (Microsoft.Storage) and top-level file shares (Microsoft.FileShares) resource models.

## Provisioned v1 Model Details

- Only for SSD premium tier.
- Minimum: 100 GiB; Maximum: 100 TiB.
- IOPS formula: MIN(3000 + 1 × ProvisionedStorageGiB, 102400)
- Throughput formula: 100 + CEILING(0.04 × ProvisionedStorageGiB) + CEILING(0.06 × ProvisionedStorageGiB)
- Supports credit-based bursting (free) and paid bursting (optional, usage-based).
- Snapshots billed at reduced rate regardless of unused provisioned space.

## Pay-as-you-go Model Details

- Only HDD (standard) storage, classic file shares.
- Three access tiers: Transaction optimized, Hot, Cool.
- Tiers differ in storage price vs. transaction price ratios.
- Transactions categorized as: Write, List, Read, Other/Protocol, Delete.
- Switching tiers incurs transaction and data retrieval charges.
- Best practice: Start in transaction optimized during migration, then optimize access tier based on post-migration usage patterns.

## Key Considerations for Cost Planning

- Use base-2 units (KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB).
- Reservations offer up to 36% discount on storage.
- Azure Files is fully managed; value-added services (Azure Backup, Azure File Sync, Microsoft Defender for Storage) have additional costs.
- Soft delete and snapshots have specific billing implications under each model.
- Storage account limits (shared across shares) require careful capacity planning for 3-5 years.
</summary>

This article from Finout (published April 20, 2026) provides a comprehensive breakdown of cloud storage pricing across the four major providers — AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle OCI — with a focus on hidden costs beyond the headline per-GB rate.

## Why Storage Costs Are Hard to Predict
Cloud storage pricing involves five distinct cost dimensions: storage capacity, API operations, data retrieval, data transfer out (egress), and replication/cross-region transfer. Real-world spend can be 2-5x higher than raw storage rates.

## Pricing Summary (May 2026, US Regions, Single-Region Redundancy)

| Provider | Hot/Standard | Infrequent Access/Cool | Cold | Archive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AWS S3 | $0.023/GB (first 50 TB) | $0.0125/GB (S3 Standard-IA) | $0.004/GB (Glacier Instant) | $0.00099/GB (Deep Archive) |
| Azure Blob | $0.018/GB (Hot, LRS) | $0.010/GB (Cool) | $0.0045/GB (Cold) | $0.00099/GB (Archive) |
| Google Cloud | $0.020/GB (Standard) | $0.010/GB (Nearline) | $0.004/GB (Coldline) | $0.0012/GB (regional Archive) |
| Oracle OCI | $0.0255/GB (Standard) | $0.015/GB (Infrequent Access) | — | $0.0026/GB (Archive) |

## Key Provider Details

**AWS S3:** Multiple tiers with volume discounts. Hidden costs include request charges (PUT $0.005/1,000; GET $0.0004/1,000), egress ($0.09/GB first 10TB), and minimum storage durations (30-180 days). A 100TB S3 Standard workload goes from $2,304/month on paper to ~$3,200 with requests and egress.

**Azure Blob:** Four-tier model with Cold tier ($0.0045/GB) splitting the difference between IA and Glacier. Redundancy multiplies costs significantly — GRS is roughly 2x LRS. A 128 KiB minimum billable object size applies to Cool, Cold, and Archive tiers.

**Google Cloud:** Simplest structure of the big four. Notable 2026 changes: Nearline multi-region pricing increased (to $0.015/GB), Archive multi-region decreased (to $0.0024/GB in US/EU). Inter-region traffic within same multi-region is free for reads.

**Oracle OCI:** Most expensive hot tier ($0.0255/GB) but includes 10 TB/month free egress and charges only $0.0085/GB beyond that — roughly 10x cheaper than AWS egress. Best for egress-heavy workloads.

## New AI Storage Pricing (2026)

**AWS S3 Vectors:** Purpose-built for vector embeddings (RAG, semantic search). $0.06/GB/month storage, $0.20/GB uploads, plus query charges. AWS claims up to 90% cost reduction vs. traditional vector DBs.

**AWS S3 Tables (Apache Iceberg):** For analytical tabular data. $0.0265/GB/month (15% above S3 Standard), plus $0.05/GB processed for maintenance operations — teams have reported 20x bill increases from forgetting this.

**Training/Inference Data:** Best practice is lifecycle policies — Standard during active training, Intelligent-Tiering/Nearline for 90 days after, Glacier/Archive after that. A 500 TB training bucket can drop from $11,500/month to ~$2,800/month with proper tiering.

## Hidden Costs
1. Egress fees (often exceed storage charges)
2. Request charges (log-heavy buckets can spend 2x on requests vs. storage)
3. Retrieval fees ($0.02-$0.05/GB on archive tiers)
4. Minimum storage durations (30-180 days)
5. Minimum object size charges (Azure 128 KiB, GCP 128 KB)
6. Redundancy costs (GRS roughly doubles rates)
7. Cross-service integration tools that also cost money

## FinOps Best Practices
1. Allocate before optimizing (use Virtual Tags for cost ownership)
2. Automate lifecycle policies
3. Monitor access patterns, not just storage size
4. Model total cost (storage + requests + egress + retrieval)
5. Apply unit economics

<summary>
This guide compares AWS Savings Plans and Reserved Instances (RIs) as of 2026 for reducing compute costs via commitment-based discounts (savings of 30-72% vs on-demand). 

**Savings Plans** (launched Nov 2019): Commit to $/hour of compute usage. Three types:
- **Compute Savings Plans** (most flexible): Covers EC2, Fargate, Lambda; any instance family, region, OS; up to 66% off (3yr all upfront).
- **EC2 Instance Savings Plans**: Locked to instance family & region; flexible on size, OS, tenancy; up to 72% off.
- **SageMaker Savings Plans**: Up to 64% off.

**Reserved Instances**: Commit to a specific instance configuration. Types include Standard RIs (locked, up to 72% off, sellable on marketplace), Convertible RIs (exchangeable, up to 66%, not sellable), and Zonal vs Regional RIs. RIs are required for services not covered by Savings Plans: RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch, Redshift, DynamoDB, MemoryDB.

**Key differences**: Compute SP offers maximum flexibility with minimal management; RIs offer deeper discounts but require active management (tracking, modifying, selling, renewing). Discount gap between Compute SP and Standard RIs is typically 3-6 percentage points.

**Recommended strategy**: Start with Compute Savings Plans at 50-60% of baseline compute spend. Add RDS/ElastiCache RIs for stable production databases. Keep 30-40% on-demand for flexibility. Review quarterly.

**Common mistakes**: Over-committing (commit to minimum sustained usage, not average), buying RIs for volatile workloads, ignoring expiring commitments, incorrect stacking of RIs and Savings Plans, and not accounting for architecture changes.

**Practical recommendation**: Compute Savings Plans for most teams (safest default). Use RIs only for database services and when maximum discount is needed with operational discipline.

---

## 1. MARKET CONTEXT AND OVERVIEW

**Cloud Market Share (Q1 2026):** AWS leads with 28-31% of the global cloud infrastructure market, followed by Microsoft Azure at 21-25%, Google Cloud Platform at 13-14%, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure at approximately 3%. Together, the Big Four hold roughly 65% of the worldwide cloud infrastructure market. Cloud spending hit $119 billion in Q4 2025 alone. The Big Three (AWS, Azure, GCP) invested over $116 billion in Q1 2026 alone on infrastructure, with AI workloads driving the majority of new capacity. Multi-cloud adoption reached 89% among enterprises, up from 76% in 2024. [Sources: Tech Insider, EffectiveSoft, CloudZero, Finout]

**2026 Pricing Changes:**
- **Google Cloud** cut compute pricing by 8% across all regions in Q1 2026. [Tech Insider]
- **GCP** also adjusted multi-region storage pricing: Nearline multi-region increased from $0.010/GB to $0.015/GB per month; Archive multi-region in US/EU decreased from $0.004/GB to $0.0024/GB per month. [CloudZero GCP Storage Pricing, Finout]
- **Azure** retired new purchases and renewals of Reserved VM Instances for select legacy VM series (Av2, Dv2/Dsv2, Dv3/Dsv3, Ev3/Esv3, F/Fs/Fsv2, G/Gs, Ls/Lsv2, etc.) effective July 1, 2026. Existing RIs honored through full term. [SpendArk, Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Community Hub, Cloud Factory]
- **Azure** introduced Smart Tier (GA April 2026) which automates blob movement between Hot, Cool, and Cold tiers. [SpendArk]
- **Azure** paused a planned 128 KiB minimum billable object size for Cool/Cold/Archive tiers on June 8, 2026, before it took effect. [SpendArk]
- **AWS Free Tier** changed July 15, 2025: new accounts now get up to $200 in credits for 6 months instead of 12 months of free tier instances. [Usage.ai, CloudZero S3]
- **OCI** eliminated all outbound data transfer charges across its full commercial footprint as of February 2026, making egress $0 across all regions, all compute shapes. [Spheron]

---

## 2. COMPUTE PRICING

### 2.1 On-Demand/Pay-As-You-Go Pricing for Comparable VM Tiers

All pricing is for Linux instances in the US East region (us-east-1 for AWS, us-central1 for GCP, East US for Azure, and US East (Ashburn) for OCI). Prices are per hour unless otherwise noted.

#### 2 vCPU / 8 GB RAM

| Provider | Instance Type | On-Demand Hourly | Monthly (730 hrs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **AWS** | m7i.large (Intel) | $0.1008/hr | ~$73.58/month |
| **AWS** | t4g.large (ARM Graviton2) | $0.0672/hr | ~$49.06/month |
| **AWS** | m7g.large (ARM Graviton4) | $0.0816/hr | ~$59.57/month |
| **Azure** | D2s v3 (Intel) | $0.096/hr | ~$70.08/month |

| **GCP** | n4-standard-2 (Intel) | $0.0907/hr | ~$66.21/month |
| **GCP** | n4d-standard-2 (AMD) | $0.0847/hr | ~$61.83/month |
| **OCI** | VM.Standard.E6 (AMD, 2 OCPU = 4 vCPU) | $0.0450/hr | ~$32.85/month |
| **OCI** | VM.Standard.A1 (ARM, 2 OCPU = 2 vCPU) | $0.0229/hr | ~$16.72/month |

**Note on OCI shapes:** 1 OCPU = 2 vCPUs for x86-based compute. So a 2 OCPU instance = 4 vCPUs. For a true 2 vCPU / 8 GB comparison on OCI, the config would be 1 OCPU / 8 GB. OCI uses flexible shapes where you can configure CPU and memory separately. Pricing for OCI is $0.0255/OCPU hour + $0.0015/GB memory hour for standard x86 VMs. [Oracle CloudZero, OCI Price List]

**Key finding from EffectiveSoft:** For a 2 CPU, 8 GB instance: AWS=$70.08/month, Azure=$70.08/month, GCP=$71.90/month, OCI=$38.69/month. [EffectiveSoft]

#### 4 vCPU / 16 GB RAM

**Key findings from shattered.io:** For 4 vCPU/16 GB on-demand, GCP is cheapest at $0.134/hr (e2-standard-4), AWS at $0.166/hr, Azure at $0.192/hr. [shattered.io]

**Key findings from EffectiveSoft:** For 16 CPU, 64 GB instance: AWS=$560.64/month, Azure=$560.64/month, GCP=$568.17/month, OCI=$309.50/month. [EffectiveSoft]

**OCI comparison from Oracle's pricing page:** Oracle claims a virtual machine (AMD, 4 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM) costs **$54/month** on OCI vs 2.1-2.3X more on AWS, Azure, GCP. [Oracle Cloud Pricing]

#### ARM Instance Pricing

All three major providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) offer ARM-based instances at approximately 20% lower on-demand pricing than equivalent x86 instances. Specific ARM examples:
- **AWS Graviton2/4:** 10-20% lower cost vs x86. m7g.large at $0.0816/hr vs m7i.large at $0.1008/hr. [Usage.ai EC2, GoCloud.io]
- **Azure Cobalt 100:** D4ps v5 at ~$0.154/hr for 4 vCPU/16 GB. [Usage.ai Cloud Pricing Comparison]
